readerTitle: Two businesses grew 7%. Only one got bigger.
caseNote: 가상 사례 (식당, 소프트웨어 회사, 가구 공방) · 모든 수치는 설명용
insight: 성장률과 수익률은 그 돈으로 살 수 있는 것으로 읽어야 하고, 기준은 전국 평균 물가가 아니라 내 사업이 실제로 사는 것들의 가격 상승이다.
misconception: 매출이 7% 늘었으면 사업이 7% 커진 것이다. 이자가 붙는 계좌에 둔 돈은 줄어들지 않는다.

sources.text: Fisher, I. (1930). The Theory of Interest. 명목 이자율과 실질 이자율의 관계 (피셔 방정식)

cards.title: Two businesses grew 7%. Only one got bigger.
body: A seaside restaurant and a small software company both closed the year with revenue up 7%. Both owners celebrated.
One of them is now running a smaller business than a year ago. The revenue line can't tell you which.

image.label: Two identical upward arrows labeled +7%, one quietly shrinking
image.brief: 왼쪽에 식당 건물, 오른쪽에 노트북 책상. 둘 위에 똑같은 "+7%" 화살표. 식당 쪽 화살표 그림자는 짧게 줄어들고 있고, 소프트웨어 쪽 그림자는 조금 길다. 실제 브랜드 로고 없음. 따뜻한 플랫 일러스트.

cards.title: Did they really grow 7%?
body: Both went from $1,000,000 to $1,070,000 in revenue. General prices across the economy rose 4% that year.
The restaurant's own costs (food, wages, rent) rose 9%. The software company's costs (mostly salaries and servers) rose 3%. How should each owner judge the year?

options.text: Both grew 7%. The revenue numbers are identical
options.feedback: Simple and easy to report, but it ignores that each dollar now buys less. Equal revenue growth hid very different years.

options.text: Both grew about 3%, after the 4% general inflation
options.feedback: A big step: you adjusted for prices. But the general figure is an average. Neither business buys the average basket.

options.text: It depends on what each business has to buy with its money
options.feedback: Right. Against its own costs, the restaurant shrank and the software company grew. Next card shows the math.

cards.title: Same 7%, three different answers.
body: The restaurant's revenue now buys about 1.8% less of the food, labor and space it runs on. It worked harder to stand still, then slipped back.

breakdown.label: Software company, after its own costs (3%)

cards.title: Nominal vs real returns
body: **Inflation** is the rise in prices over time, so the same dollar buys less. A **nominal** return is the change in dollars. A **real** return is the change in what those dollars can buy.
Quick rule: real return ≈ nominal return − inflation. For an exact answer, divide: (1 + nominal) ÷ (1 + inflation) − 1.
The economist Irving Fisher set out this link between money returns and real returns almost a century ago.

image.label: A stack of coins next to a shrinking shopping basket
image.brief: 왼쪽: 동전 더미가 "$100,000 → $104,000"로 조금 높아짐. 오른쪽: 같은 돈으로 살 수 있는 장바구니가 조금 작아짐. 가운데 라벨 "Nominal +4%" / "Real −2%". 로고 없음.

cards.title: Money can grow and still shrink.
body: A business keeps a $100,000 reserve in an account paying 4%. Inflation runs at 6%. A year later the balance reads $104,000, but it buys what about $98,100 bought before. That's a real loss of about 2%.
Small gaps add up. At 3% inflation for ten years, money that sits still loses about **a quarter** of its buying power.
When inflation is high, use division, not subtraction. A 50% return with 40% inflation is about 7% real, not 10%.

cards.title: Pick the right inflation rate.
body: The general figure is an average across what households buy. Your business has its **own inflation rate**: the price rise in what you actually pay for.
It matters for people, too. A 3% raise in a year when prices rose 5% is a pay cut of about 2% in real terms. Your team will feel it even if the payslip says "raise".
cards.softwareNote: Multi-year subscription deals at a flat price lose real value every year. Many software companies add a yearly price step to protect them, and watch salary inflation as their main cost index.

cards.title: Adjusting is a tool, not a verdict.
body: Inflation figures are estimates, and they get revised. Treat a real return as a rough guide, not a precise score.
Don't shop for the index that flatters you. Pick the one that matches your costs and stick with it, year after year.
And in low-inflation years the gap is small. The adjustment matters most when prices move fast or when you look across many years.

cards.title: Now it's a furniture workshop.
body: A hotel chain offers your workshop a three-year contract: $500,000 in year one, rising 2% each year. Your costs for wood and skilled labor have been rising about 5% a year.
What do you do?

options.text: Sign it. A built-in 2% raise every year is generous
options.feedback: The dollars grow, but your costs grow faster. By year three, each contract dollar covers about 6% less of your costs.

options.text: Sign, but link yearly increases to an index of your main input costs
options.feedback: You keep a large, steady customer and protect your real income. The trade-off is a harder negotiation up front.

options.text: Refuse. Long fixed contracts are always a trap
options.feedback: You avoid the inflation risk, but lose three years of reliable work. The problem is the price terms, not the length.

cards.title: Count growth in what money buys, not in dollars.
body: A return only means something after inflation, and the inflation that matters is the rise in your own costs.
**Try it today:** take last year's revenue growth. Divide 1 plus that growth by 1 plus the rise in your three biggest costs. Is the answer above or below 1?
